title: ENIAC
text:
CHAPTER 4. VACUUM TUBES AND THE FIRST ELECTRONIC COMPUTERS
SECTION 4.3. ENIAC

ENIAC, the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, was the machine that showed the world electronic computing worked at scale. Dedicated at the University of Pennsylvania on February 15, 1946, it filled a large room, used about 18,000 vacuum tubes and was roughly a thousand times faster than the relay calculators of Chapter 2. It was general-purpose in what it could compute, but programming it meant rewiring it by hand. That painful limitation led directly to the stored-program idea of Section 4.4.

1. The problem: firing tables

Artillery needs firing tables: for each gun, shell and charge, the elevation required to hit a target at a given range, corrected for wind, air density and so on. Each table entry requires integrating the equations of motion of a shell with air drag, a nonlinear ordinary differential equation. In simplified form:

    dvx/dt = -(k(v) / m) * v * vx
    dvy/dt = -g - (k(v) / m) * v * vy
    dx/dt  = vx
    dy/dt  = vy

where v = sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2) and k(v) is an empirically measured drag function. There is no closed-form solution, so trajectories are computed by numerical integration, stepping forward in small time steps:

    vx(t + dt) = vx(t) + (dvx/dt) * dt
    x(t + dt)  = x(t) + vx(t) * dt
    ... and so on, until the shell hits the ground.

(This is Euler's method; practical computations used more accurate schemes, but the structure, many repeated multiply-adds, is the same.)

A single trajectory took a skilled human computer with a desk calculator on the order of a day or more; a differential analyzer could do one in perhaps fifteen to thirty minutes, with limited accuracy. A firing table needed thousands of trajectories. During World War II the US Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, working with the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School of Electrical Engineering, which ran a differential analyzer and employed teams of human computers, many of them women mathematicians, fell badly behind.

2. Eckert and Mauchly

John Mauchly (1907-1980), a physicist teaching at the Moore School, had been interested in electronic calculation for weather prediction and had visited Atanasoff in 1941 (Section 4.2). In 1942 he wrote a memo proposing an electronic computer for ballistics. J. Presper Eckert (1919-1995), a brilliant young graduate engineer at the Moore School, became the project's chief engineer. Lieutenant Herman Goldstine, a mathematician serving as the Army's liaison, championed the proposal.

The construction contract was signed on June 5, 1943, and secret work began the following month under the code name "Project PX," with John Brainerd as principal investigator. Construction was complete in May 1945, too late for the war it was built for, and the machine was formally dedicated on February 15, 1946. The final cost was about $487,000. Many engineers designed individual units, among them Arthur Burks (multiplier), Harry Huskey (reader/printer), Jeffrey Chuan Chu (divider/square-rooter) and others.

3. Physical scale

By the end of its working life ENIAC contained about 18,000 vacuum tubes, 7,200 crystal diodes, several thousand relays (counts differ between sources; Wikipedia gives 6,000), 70,000 resistors, 10,000 capacitors and roughly 5 million hand-soldered joints. It weighed more than 30 short tons, was about 100 feet long, 10 feet high and 3 feet deep in total, arranged in a U shape of panels around a room, and consumed about 150 kW of electricity. Most of that power went to tube heaters and was turned into heat that needed cooling.

ENIAC used ordinary radio tube types of the day: 6SN7 dual triodes for the flip-flops in its accumulators and pentodes such as 6SJ7 and 6AC7 for logic. Special high-reliability computer tubes did not yet exist.

4. Architecture: a room full of calculators

ENIAC was not organized around a central processor and memory. It was a set of about forty panels forming functional units that operated in parallel and passed pulses to each other through cables:

  - 20 accumulators, each holding a signed 10-digit decimal number, which could add and subtract and also served as the only fast read/write storage;
  - a multiplier unit, which used four accumulators;
  - a divider/square-rooter unit, which used five accumulators;
  - three function tables, banks of 1,200 ten-way switches each, used to set up tabulated functions such as drag coefficients (effectively read-only memory set by hand);
  - a constant transmitter connected to an IBM punched-card reader, for input;
  - a printer unit driving an IBM card punch, for output;
  - an initiating unit (start, stop), a cycling unit (clock), and a master programmer unit for sequencing and loops.

So ENIAC's fast memory was just twenty 10-digit numbers. Everything else came from cards, switches or function tables.

5. How the accumulators worked: decimal ring counters

ENIAC computed in decimal. Each decimal digit of an accumulator was a ring counter of ten flip-flops (Section 4.1), arranged in a loop, with exactly one flip-flop in the "on" state. The position of the on-state represented the digit value 0-9. Each input pulse moved the on-state one position around the ring. Per digit, the circuits used 36 vacuum tubes, of which 10 were dual triodes forming the ring's flip-flops.

Addition by counting pulses. To add the digit 3 into a digit currently holding 6, send three pulses: the on-state moves 6 -> 7 -> 8 -> 9. To add 5 to 6, five pulses: 6 -> 7 -> 8 -> 9 -> 0 -> 1. When the ring passes from 9 to 0, it "wraps around" and generates a carry, which is later sent as one extra pulse to the next digit. This is the electronic equivalent of the digit wheels and carry levers of a mechanical adding machine.

Negative numbers used ten's complement. For a 10-digit accumulator, the negative of x is represented as 10^10 - x. Subtraction is addition of the complement, just as binary subtraction is addition of the two's complement (Section 2.2). Example with 3 digits for readability:

    -27 is represented as 1000 - 27 = 973
    50 + (-27): 050 + 973 = 1023 -> drop the overflow digit -> 023 = 23. Correct.

Timing. ENIAC's cycling unit generated a 100 kHz pulse train. An addition took one 200-microsecond cycle (20 pulse times), so the machine could perform 5,000 additions or subtractions per second per accumulator. Because many accumulators could run simultaneously, peak throughput was much higher. A 10-digit by 10-digit multiplication took 14 cycles, 2.8 ms, or about 357 per second; the division and square-root unit managed up to about 40 divisions or 3 square roots per second.

Compare with the Harvard Mark I's 0.3 s addition and 6 s multiplication (Section 2.4): ENIAC's addition was about 1,500 times faster and its multiplication about 2,000 times faster. A trajectory that took a human a day took ENIAC well under a minute, reportedly faster than the shell itself flew.

6. Programming by wiring

To program ENIAC, operators:

  - connected units with cables on "digit trays" (carrying numbers) and "program trays" (carrying control pulses);
  - set switches on each unit to specify its operation (for an accumulator: receive on which input, transmit or not, add or subtract, how many times to repeat);
  - set the master programmer for loops and conditional sequencing;
  - set function table switches for tabulated data.

A program was a physical configuration of the machine. Each unit, when it received a control pulse, carried out its configured operation and then emitted a pulse to trigger the next unit. In modern terms ENIAC's program was a dataflow graph of hardware units, wired by hand.

ENIAC could make decisions. The master programmer could count iterations, and a sign test on an accumulator's result could steer control pulses one way or another. So ENIAC had conditional branching and loops, and it is considered Turing complete (in the usual sense, ignoring finite memory). That puts it ahead of the Z3 and Harvard Mark I in generality. But changing to a new problem could take days of rewiring and checking, which made it a poor fit for the many different problems people soon wanted to solve.

7. The ENIAC programmers

The people who worked out how to program ENIAC, from wiring diagrams and with limited documentation, were six women selected from the Moore School's human computers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jean Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman. They learned the machine's logic in depth, designed problem setups, and debugged them, often by tracing pulses panel by panel. Betty Jennings and Betty Snyder developed the trajectory program demonstrated at the public unveiling in 1946. Their contributions were largely unrecognized for decades and have been documented more fully since the 1980s and 1990s. Several went on to important careers; Betty Snyder Holberton, for instance, wrote an early sort/merge generator and worked on UNIVAC and on programming language standards.

8. Reliability

Tube failures were the critics' great fear. The engineers' countermeasures (Section 4.1) worked: running tubes well below their ratings, careful power-up, continuous operation, and plug-in units. Eckert recalled in a 1989 interview that they "had a tube fail about every two days" and could locate the problem within about fifteen minutes. In 1954 the longest continuous run without failure was 116 hours. For an 18,000-tube machine in the 1940s, that was a remarkable engineering achievement and convinced skeptics that large electronic computers were practical.

9. What ENIAC computed

Although built for firing tables, ENIAC's first major job was for Los Alamos. John von Neumann, consultant to both the Ballistic Research Laboratory and Los Alamos, learned of ENIAC in 1944 and arranged for calculations related to the feasibility of the hydrogen bomb, which ran on the machine starting in late 1945. Later ENIAC runs for Los Alamos used the Monte Carlo method, invented by Stanislaw Ulam and developed with von Neumann and Nicholas Metropolis: simulate many random neutron histories and average them. The success of these runs helped make Monte Carlo methods a standard tool of science.

Monte Carlo deserves a note for AI students. The idea of estimating something by averaging random samples reappears throughout modern AI: Markov chain Monte Carlo in Bayesian statistics, Monte Carlo tree search in AlphaGo (Section 16.4), dropout and stochastic gradient descent in neural network training, and sampling text from language models (Chapter 19).

ENIAC also did one of the first numerical weather predictions, in 1950, by a team including Jule Charney, Ragnar Fjortoft and von Neumann.

After the war, ENIAC was moved to Aberdeen Proving Ground in 1947 and operated there until 1955. Around 1948 it was modified so that it could be programmed from instructions set on the function tables, giving it a form of stored, though read-only, program and eliminating most rewiring (Section 4.4 discusses this conversion). Parts of ENIAC are preserved at the University of Pennsylvania, the Smithsonian, and other museums.

10. Legacy

  Speed changed what was possible. A thousand-fold speedup is not just quantitative; it makes new kinds of problems feasible, such as Monte Carlo simulation and weather prediction. The same pattern repeats in AI: GPUs (Chapter 15) made deep learning feasible in a way that faster CPUs alone did not.

  The programming bottleneck. ENIAC was general but hard to program. As Eckert, Mauchly and von Neumann discussed ENIAC's successor, EDVAC, from 1944 onward, the solution became clear: store the program in fast memory, alongside data, as numbers the machine itself could read and even modify. That is the subject of Section 4.4.

  The industry. Eckert and Mauchly left Penn in 1946 to found what became the Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation, which built BINAC and UNIVAC I (delivered in 1951 to the US Census Bureau), the start of the commercial computer industry in the United States.

  Public image. Newspapers in 1946 called ENIAC a "giant brain." That metaphor, of computers as electronic brains, shaped public expectations and, a decade later, the ambitions of the founders of AI.

11. Summary

  - ENIAC (contract June 1943, completed 1945, dedicated February 15, 1946, at the Moore School) was built by Eckert, Mauchly and team for Army ballistic computations.
  - It used about 18,000 tubes, weighed over 30 tons, used about 150 kW, and cost about $487,000.
  - It computed in decimal with ring counters in 20 ten-digit accumulators, using ten's complement for negatives; it did 5,000 additions per second per accumulator and about 357 ten-digit multiplications per second.
  - It was programmed by cables and switches, had conditional branching and loops, and is considered Turing complete, but reprogramming took days.
  - Six women programmers made it work; it ran hydrogen bomb and Monte Carlo calculations and an early weather forecast, and operated until 1955.
  - Its programming bottleneck motivated the stored-program design.
